title: Biomedical Effects of Popular Phytonutrients and Their Phytochemicals: A Comprehensive Review

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Conceptual Overview of Phytonutrients
subsections.subsection_title: Defining Phytonutrients and Their Place in Plant-Based Diets
subsections.content:
Phytonutrients are non-nutrient or conditionally bioactive compounds synthesized by plants that, while not classified as essential nutrients like vitamins or minerals, can modulate human physiology through antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, immunoregulatory, and cell-signaling effects. The term encompasses diverse chemical families—including polyphenols, carotenoids, glucosinolates, organosulfur compounds, phytosterols, and phytoestrogens—typically consumed as part of whole plant foods rather than as isolated agents. Contemporary dietary literature situates these compounds within broader plant-based eating patterns, where fruits, vegetables, legumes, whole grains, nuts, seeds, herbs, and spices provide complex matrices that influence their biological activity and health relevance ref [1], ref [2], ref [3].

In plant-based diets, phytonutrients are best understood as contributors to the protective associations consistently observed between higher intake of minimally processed plant foods and lower risk of chronic disorders. Reviews of vegetables and fruit emphasize that their health effects likely arise from combined actions of fiber, micronutrients, and numerous phytochemicals rather than from single compounds alone ref [3]. Similarly, dietary patterns rich in plant foods have been linked to improved metabolic control and cardiometabolic risk profiles in type 2 diabetes management, with phytochemical density considered one mechanistic dimension of benefit ref [2]. In inflammatory bowel disease, diet-derived plant bioactives are increasingly discussed as modulators of oxidative stress, mucosal inflammation, and microbiota-related pathways, underscoring that phytonutrients act within diet-wide and host–microbe contexts ref [1].

Accordingly, defining phytonutrients in nutrition science requires a matrix-based perspective: they are characteristic bioactive constituents of plant-centered diets whose relevance depends on food source, habitual intake pattern, and interaction with other dietary components. This framing helps distinguish phytonutrients from conventional nutrients while also avoiding reductionist claims unsupported by whole-diet evidence. It also explains why epidemiologic and clinical benefits are generally strongest for diets abundant in varied plant foods, rather than for supplementation with single isolated phytochemicals ref [2], ref [3].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Conceptual Overview of Phytonutrients
subsections.subsection_title: Traditional and Historical Perspectives on Plant Bioactives
subsections.content:
Human engagement with plant bioactives long predates modern nutrition science. In classical medical systems, plants were selected not only for macronourishment but also for perceived effects on pain, inflammation, digestion, mood, and vitality, thereby foreshadowing the modern concept of phytonutrients. Reviews of traditional Chinese and Indian medicine show that complex botanical formulations were historically used for disorders involving dependence, withdrawal, and systemic imbalance, illustrating an empirical appreciation of multifunctional plant constituents even when their chemical identities were unknown ref [4].

Historical evidence from ancient Egypt similarly indicates that plant-derived materials occupied a central place in medicine, ritual, and preservation practices. Archaeological work on Egyptian canopic jars underscores how botanical substances intersected with therapeutic knowledge and embodied early practical uses of aromatic and resinous plant products, many of which are now recognized as rich in terpenoids, phenolics, and other bioactive metabolites ref [5]. More broadly, foundational analyses of ancient Egyptian medicine and Greek pharmacology document sustained reliance on herbs, oils, wines, and plant extracts for wound care, gastrointestinal disorders, and infections, linking traditional materia medica with later pharmacognostic inquiry ref [3], ref [4].

These historical traditions should not be read as direct proof of efficacy, but they provided a durable knowledge base that guided the discovery of salicylates, morphinan alkaloids, artemisinin, and many other clinically relevant natural products ref [5], ref [6], ref [7]. At the same time, modern evidence-based evaluation has highlighted the need to distinguish culturally important use from reproducible therapeutic benefit, standardization, and safety. Thus, the historical record is best viewed as both an origin of hypotheses about plant bioactives and a reminder that translation from traditional practice to validated phytonutrient use requires rigorous phytochemical and biomedical assessment ref [4], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Conceptual Overview of Phytonutrients
subsections.subsection_title: Major Classes, Sources, and Food Processing Effects
subsections.content:
Phytonutrients comprise several major chemical classes with distinct food sources and biological roles. Polyphenols include flavonoids, phenolic acids, stilbenes, and lignans, which are abundant in berries, tea, cocoa, grapes, whole grains, and many vegetables. Carotenoids such as β-carotene, lycopene, lutein, and zeaxanthin are concentrated in orange, red, and dark-green plant foods, whereas glucosinolates are characteristic of cruciferous vegetables. Other important groups include organosulfur compounds from garlic and onions, saponins from legumes and botanicals such as mate, and tocopherols/tocotrienols (vitamin E vitamers) from nuts, seeds, and vegetable oils ref [6], ref [8], ref [4], ref [5], ref [6].

Food processing can markedly alter phytonutrient content, sometimes reducing labile compounds and sometimes improving extractability. Thermal processing commonly decreases water-soluble and oxidation-sensitive phytochemicals through leaching, isomerization, and degradation, but may also disrupt cell walls and protein–matrix interactions, increasing the measurable availability of carotenoids and some phenolics ref [7], ref [7], ref [8]. For example, boiling often causes greater losses of glucosinolates and phenolics than steaming, while tomato processing can enhance lycopene bioaccessibility despite some depletion of other antioxidants ref [7], ref [9], ref [10]. Drying, fermentation, milling, and storage further reshape phytochemical profiles by enzymatic conversion, oxidation, and changes in food microstructure ref [7], ref [11].

These effects are class-specific and matrix-dependent, making source and preparation method central to nutritional interpretation. Saponins illustrate how physicochemical behavior influences processing and functionality, as their self-assembly and interfacial properties can affect stability in complex food systems ref [8]. Likewise, the biological relevance of vitamin E depends not only on content but also on the distribution of individual vitamers across plant oils and processed foods ref [6], ref [12]. Accordingly, classification of phytonutrients should be considered together with food source, matrix, and processing history rather than as a fixed compositional attribute.

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Conceptual Overview of Phytonutrients
subsections.subsection_title: Bioavailability and Delivery Challenges of Phytonutrients
subsections.content:
A central barrier to translating phytonutrients into consistent clinical benefit is their often poor and highly variable oral bioavailability. Many prominent phytochemicals, including flavonoids, curcuminoids, carotenoids, and stilbenes, exhibit low aqueous solubility, chemical instability during digestion, extensive phase I/II metabolism, efflux by intestinal transporters, and rapid systemic elimination, all of which reduce circulating concentrations of the parent compound and complicate dose–response interpretation ref [10], ref [5], ref [6]. In practice, the bioactive species reaching tissues may differ substantially from the native dietary molecule because gut microbiota- and host-derived metabolites can dominate systemic exposure ref [6], ref [7].

These constraints have stimulated formulation-focused strategies to enhance dissolution, absorption, and tissue delivery. Mechanochemical complexation has been explored to improve the solubility and apparent bioavailability of poorly water-soluble flavonoids such as kaempferol ref [9]. More broadly, lipid-based carriers, nanoemulsions, liposomes, solid lipid nanoparticles, polymeric nanoparticles, phospholipid complexes, and self-emulsifying systems have been developed to protect phytochemicals from degradation, increase intestinal residence, and promote lymphatic or transcellular uptake ref [10], ref [11], ref [8], ref [9]. Such approaches have been especially emphasized for anticancer phytochemicals whose promising in vitro effects are not readily reproduced in vivo because of pharmacokinetic limitations ref [10], ref [11].

An important conceptual refinement is that delivery in foods and herbal matrices may already be structured by nature. Natural occurring nanoparticles and multicomponent extract matrices can alter intestinal absorption through co-solubilization, transporter modulation, and synergistic interactions among constituents, suggesting that whole-food or minimally processed preparations may sometimes outperform isolated compounds ref [4]. Even so, improved delivery does not guarantee efficacy or safety; standardization, metabolite-aware pharmacokinetics, food-matrix effects, and well-designed human trials remain essential for evidence-based application of phytonutrients ref [4], ref [5], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Conceptual Overview of Phytonutrients
subsections.subsection_title: From Natural Products to Evidence-Based Use
subsections.content:
The transition from traditional plant use to evidence-based phytonutrient application requires distinguishing crude botanical preparations, isolated phytochemicals, and standardized food-derived interventions. Natural products have historically been a major source of therapeutic innovation, with a substantial fraction of approved drugs being natural products, derivatives, or inspired by natural scaffolds, underscoring the biomedical relevance of plant bioactives beyond folkloric use ref [13]. At the same time, the pharmacological promise of phytonutrients should not be conflated with proven clinical efficacy, because mechanistic activity in vitro often exceeds what is achievable in humans after digestion, metabolism, and tissue distribution.

Accordingly, evidence-based use depends on rigorous characterization of composition, reproducible manufacturing, and fit-for-purpose clinical evaluation. For botanical products, quality-by-design frameworks have been proposed to control raw material variability, authentication, contaminant risks, and batch-to-batch consistency, all of which are essential for meaningful safety and efficacy assessment ref [12]. These issues are especially important for multi-component plant matrices, where cultivar, geography, harvest conditions, storage, and processing can alter phytochemical profiles and thereby biological effects. Without such standardization, conflicting outcomes across preclinical and clinical studies may reflect product heterogeneity rather than true inconsistency of the phytonutrient itself.

An evidence-based framework therefore integrates ethnobotanical knowledge, modern analytical chemistry, pharmacokinetics, toxicology, and well-designed human trials. In practice, this means moving from descriptive claims about "antioxidant" or "anti-inflammatory" foods toward validated biomarkers, dose-response relationships, and clinically relevant endpoints. Such a pathway does not diminish the value of natural products; rather, it provides the methodological bridge by which promising phytonutrients can be translated into credible nutritional guidance, safer botanical supplements, and, in selected cases, drug discovery leads ref [12], ref [13].

subsections.section_title: Turmeric: Botanical Characteristics, Phytochemical Composition, and Biomedical Activities
subsections.subsection_title: Botanical Identity, Cultivation, and Traditional Context
subsections.content:
Turmeric is the rhizomatous perennial Curcuma longa L. of the family Zingiberaceae, a taxon whose nomenclatural identity has been clarified through formal typification to stabilize its botanical usage in pharmacognosy and medicinal plant research [1]. It is characterized by thick, branched underground rhizomes rich in yellow-orange pigments, broad lanceolate leaves arising from a pseudostem, and inflorescences typical of Curcuma species. Native to South and Southeast Asia and now cultivated widely across tropical and subtropical regions, turmeric is propagated vegetatively through rhizome pieces rather than by seed, a practice that preserves desirable agronomic and phytochemical traits [1, 3].

Cultivation outcomes are strongly shaped by edaphic and climatic factors. Comparative agronomic work in Okinawa showed that soil type materially affects growth, rhizome yield, and quality attributes of C. longa, underscoring that both productivity and bioactive composition are environmentally responsive [2]. In practice, turmeric performs best in warm, humid conditions with well-drained, fertile soils and adequate rainfall or irrigation, while post-harvest curing, boiling, drying, and polishing further influence commercial quality and downstream phytochemical consistency [2, 3]. Such variability is important for biomedical research because differences in cultivation and processing can alter extract composition and complicate cross-study standardization [2, 3].

Historically, turmeric has occupied a prominent place in Asian traditional medicine, food systems, and ritual culture. Reviews of its ethnomedical reemergence describe extensive use in Ayurveda, Siddha, and related traditions for wound care, digestive complaints, hepatic disorders, respiratory conditions, skin diseases, and inflammatory syndromes, as well as its enduring use as a spice, colorant, and ceremonial substance [3]. This long-standing traditional context has been a major driver of contemporary pharmacological and clinical interest, positioning turmeric as a paradigmatic example of a food-medicine interface with deep cultural continuity [3].

subsections.section_title: Turmeric: Botanical Characteristics, Phytochemical Composition, and Biomedical Activities
subsections.content:
The phytochemistry of turmeric (Curcuma longa L.) is dominated by two major fractions: a nonvolatile polyphenolic fraction and a volatile essential-oil fraction. The principal curcuminoids are curcumin, demethoxycurcumin, and bisdemethoxycurcumin, which together account for the characteristic yellow-orange color and much of the extensively studied bioactivity of the rhizome. Structure–activity analyses indicate that subtle modifications in methoxy substitution, conjugated diketone geometry, and phenolic hydroxyl groups can markedly influence biological performance, highlighting the importance of curcuminoid chemical architecture in determining potency and target selectivity ref [17].

Beyond curcuminoids, turmeric contains sesquiterpenes and related volatiles, notably ar-turmerone, α-turmerone, β-turmerone, curlone, and other oxygenated terpenoids that contribute to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial effects. Turmeric also yields less commonly discussed water-soluble constituents, including turmerosaccharides, which have been investigated as distinct bioactive fractions with potential functional relevance independent of curcumin ref [18]. This broader compositional view is important because whole-rhizome preparations and standardized extracts can differ substantially in pharmacological profile according to the relative abundance of curcuminoids, volatile oils, and polysaccharide-rich fractions.

Chemically, curcumin is notable for tautomerism, metal-chelating capacity, redox activity, and limited aqueous solubility, features that strongly shape both pharmacodynamics and formulation behavior. These properties have motivated the synthesis of curcumin analogues and metal complexes to improve stability, bioavailability, and target engagement ref [17], ref [19]. Accordingly, turmeric should be understood not as a single-compound botanical, but as a phytochemical matrix in which curcuminoids, turmerones, polysaccharides, and minor phenolics interact to produce the biological effects discussed in subsequent sections.

subsections.section_title: Turmeric: Botanical Characteristics, Phytochemical Composition, and Biomedical Activities
subsections.content:
Turmeric, largely through curcumin and related curcuminoids, exhibits broad anti-inflammatory activity by modulating canonical mediators such as NF-κB, COX-2, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and oxidative stress pathways. Experimental work shows that Curcuma longa, alone or in combination formulations, suppresses inflammatory signaling, including NF-κB and COX-2, supporting its mechanistic relevance in chronic low-grade and tissue-specific inflammation ref [21]. Broader reviews of curcumin likewise describe pleiotropic effects across inflammatory and immune-mediated disorders, including regulation of cytokine production, leukocyte activation, and redox-sensitive transcriptional programs ref [25].

Its immunomodulatory actions are also notable. In vivo evidence indicates that curcumin can attenuate acute graft-versus-host disease by rebalancing T-cell subsets, with effects on Th1, Th17, and regulatory T cells, suggesting that turmeric-derived compounds act not only as anti-inflammatory agents but also as immune homeostatic modulators ref [24]. This capacity to influence adaptive immune polarization helps explain the interest in curcumin for autoimmune and inflammatory conditions in which aberrant T-cell responses perpetuate tissue damage ref [25].

Musculoskeletal applications are supported by both preclinical and clinical observations. In arthritic rats, curcumin treatment improved articular cartilage features in the knee, indicating potential chondroprotective activity in inflammatory joint degeneration ref [22]. Clinically, topical curcumin reduced knee pain in older adults with osteoarthritis in a randomized placebo-controlled study ref [23]. A separate human trial reported that a formulation containing Curcuma longa rhizome extract improved knee joint function and reduced post-exercise pain in non-arthritic adults ref [20]. Collectively, these findings support turmeric as a promising adjunct for pain, functional limitation, and inflammation-associated musculoskeletal disorders, although formulation-dependent bioavailability remains a key determinant of translational efficacy ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Turmeric: Botanical Characteristics, Phytochemical Composition, and Biomedical Activities
subsections.subsection_title: Systemic Pharmacological Effects, Clinical Translation, and Safety
subsections.content:
Beyond its anti-inflammatory role, turmeric and curcumin exhibit broad systemic pharmacology involving metabolic, hepatic, hematologic, redox, and neoplastic pathways. Experimental studies indicate hepatoprotective and hematoprotective effects against toxicant-induced injury, with attenuation of oxidative stress and preservation of liver function indices in animal models ref [26]. Curcumin has also been linked to improved blood metabolites, antioxidant defenses, and immune-associated responses in livestock under heat stress, suggesting organism-wide cytoprotective activity ref [27]. Metabolically, turmeric-derived curcuminoids have been repeatedly associated with anti-hyperglycemic and insulin-sensitizing actions, including modulation of glucose uptake, adipokine signaling, and inflammatory drivers of insulin resistance ref [30].

Clinical translation, however, remains constrained by poor aqueous solubility, rapid metabolism, and limited oral bioavailability. Reviews of clinical trials suggest signals of efficacy in metabolic syndrome, arthritis, and some inflammatory disorders, but also emphasize heterogeneity in formulations, dosing, and endpoint selection, which complicates cross-study interpretation ref [28]. Curcumin has additionally attracted attention in oncology as a pleiotropic adjunct targeting proliferation, apoptosis, and redox homeostasis; notably, it can function as a biologically active iron chelator, a property that may contribute to both anticancer effects and context-dependent safety considerations ref [31].

From a safety perspective, turmeric is generally well tolerated at culinary exposure and in many supplementation studies, but concentrated extracts warrant caution. Potential herb–drug interactions are especially relevant in patients receiving anticoagulants such as warfarin, where altered bleeding risk has been discussed ref [29]. Iron chelation by curcumin also raises theoretical concern in individuals with marginal iron status or prolonged high-dose use ref [31]. Accordingly, clinical deployment increasingly favors standardized formulations, pharmacokinetic optimization, and careful patient selection to balance systemic benefits against interaction and dose-related risks ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Turmeric: Botanical Characteristics, Phytochemical Composition, and Biomedical Activities
subsections.content:
Turmeric, and especially its principal curcuminoid curcumin, exhibits broad anti-infective activity spanning antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral domains, although most evidence remains preclinical. Reviews of curcumin’s anti-infective pharmacology indicate activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, fungi, and multiple enveloped viruses through pleiotropic mechanisms that include membrane perturbation, interference with microbial adhesion and quorum-related processes, inhibition of key viral enzymes, and modulation of host inflammatory signaling that shapes pathogen replication niches ref [32], ref [33]. These effects are particularly relevant to turmeric because whole extracts may provide additive or synergistic actions beyond isolated curcumin through essential oils and minor phenolics ref [32].

Antibacterial studies support measurable growth-inhibitory effects of turmeric preparations and suggest formulation-dependent enhancement of efficacy. A mucoadhesive gastroretentive alginate bead system containing turmeric extract improved antibacterial performance in vitro, underscoring the importance of delivery technologies for poorly soluble phytochemicals ref [36]. Antifungal activity has also been documented against agriculturally and clinically relevant fungi: Curcuma longa extracts inhibited Fusarium graminearum, with mechanistic work implicating disruption of fungal cell integrity and identification of active constituents within the extract ref [37], while separate in vitro work showed concentration-dependent suppression of Candida albicans ref [38]. Although less directly about turmeric, adjacent phytochemical literature on biofilm control and sulfur-based natural antimicrobials reinforces the broader value of multi-target plant-derived anti-infectives against persistent infections ref [10], ref [40].

The antiviral literature is especially notable. Curcumin has been reviewed as a candidate antiviral against influenza viruses, herpesviruses, hepatitis viruses, HIV, and emerging RNA viruses, acting at viral attachment, entry, replication, and particle stability stages ref [33]. Experimental studies further show virucidal and replication-inhibitory effects against transmissible gastroenteritis virus in vitro ref [35], and broader natural-product analyses identify curcumin-related scaffolds as relevant leads for anti-HSV development ref [34]. Collectively, these findings position turmeric as a promising anti-infective botanical, but clinical translation is constrained by low oral bioavailability, variable extract standardization, and the current scarcity of rigorous human efficacy trials ref [32], ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Garlic and Cinnamon: Representative Phytonutrients and Their Health Effects
subsections.subsection_title: Garlic and Cinnamon as Representative Culinary Phytonutrients
subsections.content:
Garlic and cinnamon are useful exemplar culinary phytonutrients because they combine habitual dietary exposure with chemically well-defined bioactive fractions. In garlic, the organosulfur compounds alliin, allicin, ajoene, diallyl sulfide, diallyl disulfide, and S-allyl cysteine have been most intensively studied, whereas cinnamon is characterized by cinnamaldehyde, cinnamic acid, eugenol, procyanidins, and coumarin-containing polyphenolic fractions. These constituents have been linked to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, cardiometabolic, and chemopreventive activities, although potency varies substantially with cultivar, processing, and formulation [1, 2, 3, 4].

For garlic, mechanistic studies indicate that sulfur metabolites modulate xenobiotic metabolism, suppress NF-kappaB-dependent inflammatory signaling, enhance endogenous antioxidant defenses, and influence apoptosis and cell-cycle control [1, 2]. Human evidence, while heterogeneous, suggests modest benefits for blood pressure, serum lipids, and vascular function, particularly with standardized aged garlic preparations and garlic powder products [5, 6]. Epidemiologic and translational literature has also supported a broader role for Allium vegetable intake in cancer prevention, although causality remains difficult to establish because of confounding diet and lifestyle factors [2, 7].

Cinnamon has been widely investigated as a functional spice in metabolic health. Polyphenol-rich extracts and cinnamaldehyde-containing preparations have been reported to improve insulin signaling, delay gastric emptying, reduce postprandial glycemia, and attenuate oxidative and inflammatory stress in preclinical models and selected clinical studies [3, 4, 8, 9]. Meta-analytic evidence suggests small but potentially meaningful improvements in fasting blood glucose and lipid indices, but results are inconsistent across trials because of differences in species, dose, duration, and background therapy [10, 11]. Safety is also important: Cassia cinnamon may provide higher coumarin exposure, raising concerns about hepatotoxicity with chronic excessive use, whereas Ceylon cinnamon is generally preferred for long-term dietary applications [12].

Taken together, garlic and cinnamon illustrate how common culinary plants can serve as representative phytonutrients at the food-medicine interface. Their value in dietary prevention likely derives from repeated low-dose exposure to multi-target phytochemicals rather than single-compound pharmacology, underscoring the importance of standardization, dose definition, and rigorous clinical validation in future survey literature [1, 3, 5, 10].

subsections.section_title: Garlic and Cinnamon: Representative Phytonutrients and Their Health Effects
subsections.content:
Cinnamon has attracted attention as a source of anticancer phytonutrients, particularly cinnamaldehyde derivatives and polyphenol-rich bark extracts. Experimental studies indicate that these constituents can suppress tumor cell growth through apoptosis induction, redox perturbation, cell-cycle arrest, and interference with DNA-processing enzymes. In cervical cancer cells, an aqueous extract of Cinnamomum cassia bark induced apoptosis together with loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, supporting a mitochondria-dependent mechanism of cytotoxicity ref [41].

Among defined cinnamon phytochemicals, 2-methoxycinnamaldehyde from Cinnamomum verum is especially notable because it showed dual anti-topoisomerase I and II activity in hepatocellular carcinoma SK-Hep-1 cells and also demonstrated antitumor efficacy in vivo, suggesting a broader pharmacological range than nonspecific antioxidant effects alone ref [42]. This is important because topoisomerase-directed actions place cinnamon-derived aldehydes within a mechanistically credible anticancer framework, linking phytochemical structure to direct interference with tumor-cell DNA replication and survival pathways ref [42].

Taken together, current evidence supports cinnamon as a promising reservoir of lead anticancer agents rather than as a clinically validated anticancer therapy. The available studies remain largely preclinical and are dominated by cell-line and animal models, with variation in species source, extraction method, and phytochemical standardization limiting cross-study comparability ref [41], ref [42]. Accordingly, future work should prioritize bioactive-compound quantification, pharmacokinetic characterization, toxicity profiling, and well-designed translational studies to determine whether cinnamon-derived phytochemicals can be developed into reproducible adjunctive or standalone anticancer interventions.

Beyond commonly discussed fruits and culinary herbs, several medicinal plants provide dense and pharmacologically distinctive phytonutrient repertoires. Green tea is a major source of catechins, particularly epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), which has been linked to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cardiometabolic benefits in both mechanistic and clinical literature ref [43], ref [44]. Cocoa supplies flavan-3-ols such as epicatechin that improve endothelial function and vascular responsiveness ref [45]. Pomegranate contributes ellagitannins and anthocyanins with reported antiatherogenic and anti-inflammatory activities ref [46]. Garlic and cruciferous vegetables are also notable: organosulfur compounds from garlic and isothiocyanates derived from glucosinolates, especially sulforaphane from broccoli sprouts, have shown chemopreventive and cytoprotective effects through redox-sensitive signaling and phase II enzyme induction ref [47], ref [48].

Spice-derived phytonutrients represent another important medicinal source. Curcumin from turmeric has been extensively investigated for modulation of NF-kB, cytokine signaling, and oxidative stress pathways, although bioavailability remains a practical limitation ref [49]. Ginger rhizome contains gingerols and shogaols with evidence for antiemetic, anti-inflammatory, and metabolic effects ref [50]. Cinnamon polyphenols and procyanidins have been associated with improved insulin sensitivity and glycemic control in selected studies, albeit with heterogeneity across preparations and trials ref [51]. These sources illustrate that the medicinal relevance of phytonutrients depends not only on compound class, but also on matrix effects, absorption, metabolism, and habitual intake patterns.

A further group of botanicals contributes specialized phytochemicals with emerging translational value. Soy isoflavones, especially genistein and daidzein, have attracted attention for endocrine-modulating, cardiometabolic, and bone-related actions ref [52]. Grape skins and red wine provide resveratrol and related stilbenes that influence inflammatory, vascular, and mitochondrial pathways, though clinical efficacy appears dose- and formulation-dependent ref [53]. Milk thistle is a classic medicinal source of the flavonolignan mixture silymarin, widely studied for hepatoprotective effects ref [54]. Ginkgo biloba leaves contain terpene lactones and flavonol glycosides with reported neurovascular and antioxidant activities ref [55], while olive leaves and extra-virgin olive oil supply hydroxytyrosol and oleuropein, compounds implicated in vascular protection and oxidative stress reduction ref [56]. Collectively, these additional sources broaden the therapeutic landscape of phytonutrients beyond staple produce and support a more inclusive survey of diet-derived bioactive agents.

subsections.section_title: Synthesis of Findings and Summary of Favorable Effects
subsections.subsection_title: Rule of Five as a Framework for Favorable Drug-Like Properties
subsections.content:
Within surveys of biomass-derived phytonutrients, Lipinski’s Rule of Five remains a pragmatic first-pass filter for anticipating oral drug-likeness. The framework links successful absorption and permeation to four empirical boundaries: molecular weight not exceeding 500 Da, cLogP not exceeding 5, no more than 5 hydrogen-bond donors, and no more than 10 hydrogen-bond acceptors; compounds violating more than one rule are less likely to show favorable oral exposure [1,2]. Although originally derived from synthetic and semi-synthetic drug datasets, the Rule of Five has become a common benchmark for triaging phytochemicals during lead identification because it provides an interpretable bridge between structure and developability [1-3].

For popular phytonutrients and their constituent phytochemicals, the Rule of Five is especially useful as a comparative framework rather than an absolute exclusion criterion. Many low-molecular-weight phenolics, simple terpenoids, alkaloids, and organosulfur compounds satisfy these thresholds and therefore align with desirable permeability and formulation prospects [3-6]. By contrast, several glycosylated flavonoids, tannin-related polyphenols, and highly oxygenated natural products frequently exceed hydrogen-bonding or molecular-weight limits, helping explain recurrent challenges in intestinal uptake and systemic exposure despite strong in vitro bioactivity [4,7-9]. In this sense, Rule-of-Five screening helps distinguish intrinsically tractable phytochemical scaffolds from those that may require deglycosylation, prodrug design, nanoformulation, or alternative delivery routes [5,8,10].

Importantly, contemporary medicinal chemistry treats the Rule of Five as a heuristic embedded within a broader developability assessment. Natural products often occupy structurally complex, stereochemically rich regions of chemical space, and some clinically useful agents intentionally fall outside canonical limits while retaining efficacy through transporter effects, active uptake, or non-oral administration [3,11-13]. Accordingly, for green-solvent-derived phytonutrients, Rule-of-Five compliance should be interpreted alongside polarity, solubility, metabolic stability, and target engagement. Even so, as a synthesis tool in this review, the framework remains valuable for summarizing why certain phytochemicals repeatedly emerge as more favorable starting points for discovery and translational optimization [1,3,12,13].

subsections.section_title: Synthesis of Findings and Summary of Favorable Effects
subsections.subsection_title: Measured Physicochemical Evidence Supporting Successful Discovery Outcomes
subsections.content:
Measured physicochemical data provide a stronger basis for judging discovery success than rule-based classification alone. Analyses of marketed oral drugs and development candidates show that favorable outcomes are most consistently associated with balanced, experimentally grounded properties—especially moderate lipophilicity, limited but sufficient polarity, and molecular size compatible with passive permeability and acceptable solubility—rather than strict compliance with any single cutoff ref [58]. In this sense, measured descriptors such as logD, aqueous solubility, pKa, polar surface area, and permeability translate the Rule of Five from a heuristic into an evidence-based framework for triaging bioactive phytochemicals.

Appraisals of discovery datasets indicate that compounds with lower measured lipophilicity generally exhibit improved developability, because excessive logP/logD is linked to poor solubility, high metabolic turnover, promiscuity, and safety liabilities ref [58]. This principle is highly relevant for phytonutrient-derived leads, many of which combine aromatic scaffolds with multiple hydroxyl or methoxy substituents. For such compounds, direct measurement is essential because ionization, tautomerism, and intramolecular hydrogen bonding can cause calculated properties to misrepresent true exposure-relevant behavior. When measured solubility and permeability are jointly optimized, successful candidates more often achieve the practical balance required for oral absorption and downstream formulation ref [58].

Accordingly, favorable discovery outcomes for biomass-derived phytochemicals are best supported by integrated physicochemical profiling rather than structural novelty alone. Compounds advancing successfully tend to occupy a constrained multidimensional space in which measured lipophilicity, solubility, ionization state, and permeability are mutually compatible with absorption and medicinal chemistry tractability ref [58]. This evidence-based emphasis is especially valuable in natural-product research, where chemically attractive scaffolds may otherwise be overvalued despite suboptimal developability.

subsections.section_title: Synthesis of Findings and Summary of Favorable Effects
subsections.subsection_title: Pharmacokinetic Advantages of Biomass-Derived Compounds Obtained via Green Solvents
subsections.content:
Biomass-derived phytonutrients isolated with green solvents can exhibit pharmacokinetic advantages that extend beyond sustainability considerations. By avoiding toxic residual solvents and enabling tunable solvent polarity, green extraction often preserves labile phenolics, terpenoids, alkaloids, and lipid-soluble micronutrients in forms more compatible with downstream absorption and formulation, thereby improving apparent solubility, chemical stability, and intestinal availability relative to harsher conventional processes [1]. In practice, these effects are especially relevant for phytochemicals whose clinical translation is constrained by low aqueous solubility, rapid presystemic metabolism, or poor membrane permeability.

Mechanistically, green solvents such as supercritical CO2, ethanol, natural deep eutectic solvents, and selected ionic-liquid-inspired systems can enrich target compounds while limiting thermal degradation and oxidation, which helps maintain molecular integrity required for favorable ADME behavior [1]. For example, supercritical CO2 extraction has been widely associated with enhanced recovery of nonpolar bioactives such as carotenoids, tocopherols, phytosterols, and essential oil constituents, often yielding cleaner extracts that are more readily incorporated into lipid-based delivery systems known to improve oral bioavailability. Likewise, ethanol- and eutectic-based extracts may retain co-occurring amphiphilic matrices that act as natural solubilizers or permeability enhancers, potentially increasing dissolution and reducing precipitation in gastrointestinal environments [1].

From a drug-likeness perspective, the pharmacokinetic value of green-solvent-derived biomass fractions lies in producing chemically consistent, low-contaminant extracts that better support predictable absorption and safer repeated exposure [1]. Such extracts can also facilitate lower excipient burdens and improved compatibility with nanoformulations, self-emulsifying systems, or phospholipid complexes used to overcome first-pass loss and short half-life. Accordingly, green extraction should be viewed not only as an environmentally preferable upstream step, but also as a practical enabler of favorable pharmacokinetic performance in phytonutrient discovery and translational development [1].
